content.text:
The audit round has given me what I need, but not the way I planned it. Most inventory lanes stopped after 0–3 files, even with narrow scopes. They were honest about it, but per-item judgment across about 72k lines of Source is more than a Terra turn can carry.

So I built the checklist mechanically instead. `desktop/gpui/tools/parity-inventory/extract.ts` is committed on the integration branch as `a9a25d86`. It parses all 173 Source component and route files and lists 8,744 items: every handler, control, ARIA attribute, rendered state, piece of copy, handled key, persisted key and animation. It also checks whether each user-visible string exists anywhere in the native Rust.

**Overall, 36% of Source's copy exists natively.** By area:

| Mostly unported | Partly ported | Mostly there |
|---|---|---|
| instruments 9%, desk/usage 0–20%, Settings 13–19%, living desk 17%, Live voice 12%, speech player 16%, folio menu 24%, dialogs/toasts ~0% | in-flow 33%, writing tools 30%, personas 44%, onboarding 57%, House 58% | editor 61%, rubric 61%, revisions 74%, citations 76%, comments 80% |

**Next is the port round.** I'll run about 13 Terra port lanes, each owning one area's native modules and using that area's extracted items as its checklist. Each one adds capture states and proves the result with the parity harness against the browser. They'll build on E2B, since a local build takes about 12 GB and only 39 GB is free. So the port lanes start as soon as the remote-runner lane reports. The harness lane is also close to done.

**Public pages:** landing, pricing, docs, blog, FAQ, terms, privacy and downloads will open in the system browser rather than being rebuilt natively, unless you want those native too.

is normalised to 0–1. The differing-pixel percentage uses a 2% fuzz.

need equivalent Source seeding in the driver's `seed`.

input.content:
# Port lanes: shared rules

Each port lane makes one area of the native desktop app
(`desktop/gpui/src`) match Source (the web app, `src/`) exactly at
1280 × 860. "Exactly" covers layout, spacing, type, colour, copy, states,
interactions, keyboard and persistence. Source wins wherever the two differ.
Native-only behaviour stays only where the platform needs it.

## Start

```sh
git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio
```

Read `desktop/gpui/ARCHITECTURE.md`, which covers module ownership, the
UTF-16 rules and the coordinator pattern, and `desktop/gpui/tools/parity/README.md`.

## Your checklist

1. **The complete list.** Run
   `bun desktop/gpui/tools/parity-inventory/extract.ts --out /tmp/parity-<lane>`,
   then filter `/tmp/parity-<lane>/items.jsonl` to the Source files in your
   scope. Every handler, control, ARIA attribute, rendered state, piece of
   copy, handled key, persisted key and motion class in those files must end
   up matched in native. `copyNative: true` only means the string exists
   somewhere in native, not that the surface matches.
2. **Earlier findings.** Use the `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/<area>.json`
   file your lane names, if it has one. It holds `file:line`-cited findings
   from the audit round. They are a head start, not the full list.

Keep `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/progress/<lane>.json` current. It is an
array of `{item_id, status: "done"|"blocked"|"not-applicable", native_ref, note}`
for every checklist item in scope. Commit it with your code.

## How to work

- Go surface by surface. Port the markup structure, styles (resolve Source's
  Tailwind/CSS to exact values), copy, states and interactions. Then add
  tests and capture states, then commit, then go on to the next surface.
- **Commit after every surface** with
  `devenv shell -- git commit -m "<plain English>"`. The pre-commit hook needs
  `prek`, which only exists inside devenv. Do not push.
- **Do not stop early.** Keep going until every item in scope is done,
  blocked (with the exact reason) or not applicable (with the reason). If you
  run low on room, commit and end with a precise list of what remains.
- **No fake success.** Do not ship a control that pretends to work. If a
  feature needs a backend transport that native does not have, build the
  transport if your lane owns it. Otherwise render Source's own
  unavailable/offline state and mark the item blocked, naming the transport.

## Files you may touch

- Your lane's feature modules and its own `src/app/<feature>_coordinator.rs`.
- **Shared host files**, kept as small as possible and in one block with a
  `// <lane>` comment: `src/app.rs`, `src/app/room_layout.rs`, `src/main.rs`,
  `src/lib.rs`, `tools/capture-native.py`, `tools/parity/states.json`, and
  theme or chrome. Never reformat or reorder code you do not own.
- New crates are allowed only if your lane truly needs one. Name it in the
  report, because `Cargo.lock` conflicts land on the coordinator.

## Proving it

- **Capture states.** For each surface and important state in your scope, add
  a native capture state in `src/main.rs`, `App::set_capture_state` and
  `tools/capture-native.py`. Add the matching Source driver in
  `tools/parity/drivers/<state>.ts`, and append the state to
  `tools/parity/states.json`. Seed panel data identically on both sides.
  When you have checked the content is the same, set `verified: true`.
- **Pixel parity.** Run the harness for your states and iterate until each one
  is under 1% differing pixels. Anything left must be a named, explained
  residual such as font hinting or antialiasing.
- **Behaviour.** Behaviour a screenshot cannot show (keys, focus, persistence,
  undo, async states) needs mounted `ui-tests` or library tests.

## Builds run remotely

This machine has little disk for many parallel builds. Run every
`ui-tests`/desktop build, test and capture on E2B:

input.title: Port: sign-in, account identity, sync, sharing, publishing
input.task:
Lane `account`. First run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio`, then read and follow `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/PORT_LANES.md`. It is the contract for this work: checklist, commits, proving, remote builds and report. Also read `docs/notorganic-native-identity.md`.

**Scope (Source).**
- `src/components/auth/**`: the account menu's signed-in parts, sign-in, avatar and initials, sign-out, and the sign-in toast.
- `src/routes/signin/**` and `src/routes/auth/**`.
- `src/components/collaboration/**`: the share dialog, roles, presence and invitations.
- The sync status indicator and its six states, the last-saved label and tooltip, conflicts, the outbox, and shared folios.
- Writer-owned publishing and `src/components/profile/**`.

**Earlier findings:** `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/auth.json` (62 items), `sync-share.json` (22 items) and `chrome.json` (account items). The top gaps:
- No mounted sign-in or redirect, and no registered trusted callback.
- No session restore or expiry handling.
- No signed-in identity and no sign-out.
- No invitations or shared folios.
- The sync indicator is fixed to local-only.

**What to build: the trusted auth transport.** The prepared Bun SDK session boundary (`desktop/gpui/tools/connected/`) already does redemption, restore and sign-out, but nothing mounted uses it, and the native capability flag is false.
- Mount it: system-browser sign-in with a registered callback, then session restore, expiry and sign-out.
- Expose an authenticated session interface that other lanes consume. The `desk` lane needs it for wallet/usage, `live-voice` for credentials, and `settings` for hosted AI.
- Then wire sync (outbox, CAS, conflict, already prepared in `native_accounts/`), sharing and publishing over it.

**Native modules you own:** `native_accounts/**`, `native_collaboration/**`, `tools/connected/**`, and the account menu's signed-in parts.

**Capture states:** `account-signed-in`, `account-loading`, `account-redirecting`, `account-session-expired`, `account-invitations`, `account-shared`, `share-dialog`, `sync-syncing`, `sync-conflict`, `sync-offline`, `signin-toast`. Prove the flows with a hermetic fake-backend test.

**Native modules you own:** the `dossier*.rs` files, `dossier_conversation/`, the onboarding modules, and `tools/semantic-*.generated.ts`.

**Capture states:**
- Existing and yours: `dossier`.
- Add: `dossier-format`, `dossier-conversation`, `dossier-refine`, `dossier-filing`, `onboarding-interview`, `starter-document`, `starter-document-imported`.

input.title: Port: import/export, document exchange, backups
input.task:
Lane `exchange`. First run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio`, then read and follow `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/PORT_LANES.md`. It is the contract for this work: checklist, commits, proving, remote builds and report.

**Scope (Source).**
- Every import and export format and every entry point: `src/utils/exchange.ts`, `folio-export.ts` and every UI that calls them.
- Formats: Typst, HTML, Markdown (source-aware), plain text, Word (.docx) import and export, PDF and backups.
- Entry points: file pickers, drag-in, paste-import, and replace-active vs add-imported-copy.
- Revision persistence (`src/utils/revision-history.ts`) and IDB-compatible storage, with unknown fields kept.

**Earlier findings:** `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/exchange.json`:
- Word import and export are missing.
- Source-aware Markdown and text export differ.
- Replacing the active folio differs from adding an imported copy.

**Native modules you own:** `exchange.rs`, `storage`, `manuscript`, `revisions` storage, and the document helper's conversion entry points (`tools/build-helper.ts` and its TS sources) where native reuses Source's converters.

**Proof:** proof is mainly behavioural.
- Write round-trip tests that compare native output bytes with Source's converters on the same fixtures, for every format.
- Add capture states for any visible picker, progress or error UI: `export-menu`, `import-error`, `import-replace-confirm`.

input.title: Port: narration, speech player, voice recorder
input.task:
Lane `narration`. First run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio`, then read and follow `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/PORT_LANES.md`. It is the contract for this work: checklist, commits, proving, remote builds and report.

**Scope (Source).**
- Read-aloud and narration: `src/utils/speech.ts`, `speech-splitter.ts`, `supertonic-tts.ts`, `browser-inference.ts`, provider voices (OpenAI, Fish), and the voice cast for personas.
- `src/components/ui/global-speech-player.tsx`, `speak-button.tsx`, `speech-transport.tsx` and `voice-recorder.tsx`.
- Every read-aloud entry point in the editor and panels.

**Earlier findings:**
- `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/editor.json`: read-aloud is disabled natively, and the narration player isn't mounted.
- `voice.json`.

**What to build:**
- **Audio pipeline.** Native already has `native_audio/` (PCM, segments, transport state, cache, alignment) and a real CPAL device backend (`native_audio/device.rs`, feature `native-audio-device`). Build the native TTS pipeline:
  - local Supertonic, which native can run through ONNX Runtime; add the crate and name it in the report;
  - provider TTS over HTTPS for configured providers.
- **Player and recorder.** Mount the speech player with exactly Source's controls: play/pause/seek/cancel, progress, voice and errors. Mount the recorder using the device input.
- **Public API.** Expose a simple player API or event that other lanes call to speak text.
- **Microphone permission.** If something can't be verified on this machine, test with the device backend's ignored hardware tests on the remote runner, or explain why not.

**Native modules you own:** `native_audio/**` except Live voice, plus new `narration/` and player view modules.

**Capture states:** `read-aloud`, `narration-loading`, `narration-playing`, `narration-paused`, `narration-error`, `voice-recorder`, `voice-recorder-recording`.

input.title: Port: Live voice desk with local and hosted transports
input.task:
Lane `live-voice`. First run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio`, then read and follow `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/PORT_LANES.md`. It is the contract for this work: checklist, commits, proving, remote builds and report.

**Scope (Source).**
- `src/components/ui/live-voice-desk*`.
- `src/utils/live-voice.ts`, `live-voice-contract.ts`, `live-voice-workspace.ts` and `live-voice-audio.ts`.
- The relay protocol in `scripts/live-voice-relay.mjs`.
- The full desk: connect, consent, credit check, transcript and turns, mute, level meter, client delegations (edit proposals with apply/discard, find, research, open panel), sources, and every error and close message.

**Earlier findings:** `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/voice.json`. The native Talk control is disabled, and there is no mounted desk, credentials, consent, websocket or receipt settlement.

**What to build:**
1. **The native desk UI, exactly as Source.** The `find-compositor` lane makes the compositor's Talk control dispatch an event; handle it.
2. **The hosted transport.** Make a native websocket connection to the Not Organic gateway `/v1/live/sessions` with the same DPoP/idempotency/budget handshake the relay builds. Credentials come from the account session, which the `account` lane owns. Build against an interface, and render Source's sign-in-required state when there is no session.
3. **A local transport.** Use a local realtime speech model on loopback, with LFM3-Audio from Liquid AI as the target. Investigate what local server and protocol it exposes, and adapt to Source's event contract. If a usable local runtime isn't available yet, say exactly what is missing.
4. **Audio.** Use `native_audio::live_voice` plus the CPAL device backend for mic and playback.

Add a tungstenite-style websocket crate if needed, and name it.

**Native modules you own:** `native_audio/live_voice.rs` and new `live_voice/` modules.

**Capture states:** `live-voice-desk`, `live-voice-connecting`, `live-voice-listening`, `live-voice-proposal`, `live-voice-error`, `live-voice-signed-out`. Prove the protocol with a hermetic fake gateway test.

input.title: Port: sign-in, account identity, sync, sharing, publishing
input.task:
Lane `account`. First run `git merge --ff-only feat/native-port-ai-audio`, then read and follow `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/PORT_LANES.md`. It is the contract for this work: checklist, commits, proving, remote builds and report. Also read `docs/notorganic-native-identity.md`.

**Scope (Source).**
- `src/components/auth/**`: the account menu's signed-in parts, sign-in, avatar and initials, sign-out, and the sign-in toast.
- `src/routes/signin/**` and `src/routes/auth/**`.
- `src/components/collaboration/**`: the share dialog, roles, presence and invitations.
- The sync status indicator and its six states, the last-saved label and tooltip, conflicts, the outbox, and shared folios.
- Writer-owned publishing and `src/components/profile/**`.

**Earlier findings:** `desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/auth.json` (62 items), `sync-share.json` (22 items) and `chrome.json` (account items). The top gaps:
- No mounted sign-in or redirect, and no registered trusted callback.
- No session restore or expiry handling.
- No signed-in identity and no sign-out.
- No invitations or shared folios.
- The sync indicator is fixed to local-only.

**What to build: the trusted auth transport.** The prepared Bun SDK session boundary (`desktop/gpui/tools/connected/`) already does redemption, restore and sign-out, but nothing mounted uses it, and the native capability flag is false.
- Mount it: system-browser sign-in with a registered callback, then session restore, expiry and sign-out.
- Expose an authenticated session interface that other lanes consume. The `desk` lane needs it for wallet/usage, `live-voice` for credentials, and `settings` for hosted AI.
- Then wire sync (outbox, CAS, conflict, already prepared in `native_accounts/`), sharing and publishing over it.

**Native modules you own:** `native_accounts/**`, `native_collaboration/**`, `tools/connected/**`, and the account menu's signed-in parts.

**Capture states:** `account-signed-in`, `account-loading`, `account-redirecting`, `account-session-expired`, `account-invitations`, `account-shared`, `share-dialog`, `sync-syncing`, `sync-conflict`, `sync-offline`, `signin-toast`. Prove the flows with a hermetic fake-backend test.

content.text:
The port round is running: 16 Terra lanes, each in its own worktree, plus the remote-runner lane finishing up.

**Set up first, on `feat/native-port-ai-audio`:**
- **Parity harness** (merged, then restructured in `be70a50e`). Each state now has its own browser driver file, so every lane adds drivers for its own surfaces without touching shared code. Native capture already works for all 39 existing states. Browser-vs-native pairs are scored even before their content has been confirmed identical; the report marks those as unverified.
- **E2B remote runner** (merged; the lane is finishing its end-to-end proof). Each lane builds, tests and captures in its own sandbox, and keeps its build cache between runs.
- **Shared lane rules** (`desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/PORT_LANES.md`). This gives every lane the same rules:
  - **Checklist:** the mechanical checklist for its files, plus the audit findings.
  - **Progress:** a progress file for every item.
  - **Rules:** commit after each surface, and no controls that pretend to work.
  - **Proof:** under 1% differing pixels per state (or an explained leftover), plus behaviour tests.
  - **Builds:** run remotely.

**The 16 lanes:**

| Writing surface | Panels | Projects | Connected |
|---|---|---|---|
| find, compositor and formatting | Settings (all sections, AI wiring) | chrome, folio menu, House, dialogs and toasts | narration and speech player |
| Typst views, pagination, Zen | instruments and brief | Dossier and onboarding | Live voice (hosted and local LFM3) |
| insert menu and forms | desk, usage, wallet, data controls | import/export | sign-in, sync, sharing, publishing |
| input, clipboard, history | in-flow and writing tools; board/Cast/personas; Rubric/Apparatus/Marginalia/Versions | | |

Lanes that depend on each other connect through events or interfaces, not shared edits. For example, Talk → Live voice, read-aloud → narration, and the account session → desk, Live voice and hosted AI. Public pages (pricing, docs, legal and so on) open in the system browser.

Lanes will stop early, as they did in the audit round. I'll keep sending each one back until its checklist is finished, then merge and fix conflicts in the shared host files.

The typst lane also got interrupted mid-remote-build, possibly because the E2B runner is slow on cold gpui builds, so I should suggest running the remote build in the background while continuing other work, or checking its status rather than blocking on it. I also want to verify whether the remote runner is functioning at all, since other port lanes might be stalled waiting on it — local `cargo check --no-default-features` could give faster compile feedback in the meantime.

Disk space is tight: 61G free won't support 16 lanes at ~12GB each locally, and even sharing a CARGO_TARGET_DIR wouldn't help much since cargo's build-directory lock serializes concurrent builds. Vendored gpui path dependencies would also rebuild separately per worktree since their fingerprints include the source path, so there's little artifact sharing benefit there — only registry deps would be shared. This makes relying on the E2B runner more appealing, so I want to check the runner lane's status and look at live E2B sandboxes to see if lanes are actually using it before responding to the user.

The simplest approach would be running the runner locally in the background with nohup so it keeps working while the sandbox handles the actual task, then checking the log afterward — no code changes needed, just backgrounding the process. I'm wondering though whether Codex agents actually continue their turn after spawning a background process, since the original problem was they ran things in the foreground and got stuck waiting.

I should also think about adding a lightweight wrapper script or package.json command to make backgrounding trivial, though a simple shell one-liner in the docs might suffice. There's also a build concern: with CARGO_BUILD_JOBS limited to 2 to avoid OOM, a cold build of gpui and typst could take longer than the sandbox's one-hour lifetime, so I need to think about whether a resumed run with cached build artifacts solves this, or whether warming a shared cache via a seed sandbox is necessary — though E2B's lack of shared filesystems between sandboxes complicates that.

A better approach might be baking a prebuilt target directory into the E2B template itself, running the build during template creation so each lane sandbox starts warm and only needs an incremental rebuild of the desktop crate. I should check on the runner lane's status since it may have already pushed a relevant commit, and consider asking it to bake this warm target into the template. I also need to watch out for cargo fingerprint issues tied to file mtimes being preserved through tar extraction, which could cause unnecessary rebuilds.

The vendored gpui path dependency is especially concerning here since its mtime fingerprint would force a full rebuild if source timestamps don't line up with build outputs, and that crate is massive. Forcing an artificially old mtime on everything via tar wouldn't work either, since that would make even genuinely changed files appear fresh and skip rebuilding when they shouldn't.

What I actually need is unchanged files to keep old mtimes while changed files get fresh ones. I could stage the extraction and content-compare against what's already in /root/work, only touching files that actually differ -- which also benefits warm lanes, since the current approach of wiping and re-extracting already preserves stable local mtimes for unchanged files, meaning warm lanes are incidentally already incremental. The template-prebuilt path just needs this same content-aware sync logic layered in.

But the more pressing issue right now is the stalled lanes blocking on the remote run instruction. content.content:
# Remote GPUI builds (experimental)

With Bun installed and `skate get e2b_api_key@secrets` configured, run `bun run desktop.gpui.remote <worktree> --lane <unique-name> -- <command>`, for example `bun run desktop.gpui.remote . --lane alice -- devenv shell -- cargo test --locked --features ui-tests --manifest-path desktop/gpui/Cargo.toml settings`. Commands run inside `devenv shell`; an explicit `devenv shell --` is also accepted. Add `--pull 'desktop/gpui/target/parity/**'` before `--` to retrieve files; absolute paths such as `/tmp/q.png` are saved under `tmp/q.png` in the worktree. Lanes pause after a run and preserve Cargo and Nix caches; use a different lane per concurrent agent, `bun run desktop.gpui.remote list` to inspect them, and `bun run desktop.gpui.remote stop alice` to destroy one. Without a lane the sandbox is destroyed. `--keep` is accepted with a lane. Set `E2B_API_KEY` to override skate and `TWYNE_E2B_TEMPLATE` to select another template. Each sync includes all files reported by `git ls-files -co --exclude-standard` except `target` and `node_modules`, including unignored untracked files; inspect those files before sending a worktree to a third party.

Build the template remotely with `E2B_API_KEY="$(skate get e2b_api_key@secrets)" bun desktop/gpui/tools/remote/template.ts`. Capacity errors retry with jitter for up to 20 minutes. The runner defaults Cargo to two jobs; pass `env CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=N` as the command to override it. On the one-hour deadline, a new lane automatically pauses its filesystem; the in-flight command stops and must be explicitly rerun to reuse its completed Cargo artifacts. The current account accepts 8 vCPU, 8 GiB RAM, a 25,600 MiB minimum free-disk request and one-hour sandbox lifetimes. The template installs Nix and devenv; the project lock supplies the Rust toolchain and libraries when the shell is first entered. Lane names are not an atomic distributed lock: never launch concurrent runs using the same name. The source snapshot has no Git metadata, and commands that require a Git repository will fail. The full checkout is transferred on every run; large unignored assets make sync slow. This runner is experimental until the full test and capture have passed on this account.

p='desktop/gpui/fixtures/parity/PORT_LANES.md'; s=open(p).read()
start=s.index('## Builds run remotely'); end=s.index('## Final report')
new='''## Builds run remotely and never block you

This machine has little disk, so every `ui-tests`/desktop build, test and
capture runs on E2B. **Remote jobs are detached. Start one, keep coding, and
check back later.** Never sit in a foreground remote command; that is how
earlier lanes ended their turn with nothing to show.

```sh
# Start: syncs your worktree; returns immediately.
bun run desktop.gpui.job start . --lane <lane> --pull 'desktop/gpui/target/parity/**' -- \\
  bash -c 'bun run desktop.gpui.build-helper && \\
  cargo build --locked --features ui-tests --manifest-path desktop/gpui/Cargo.toml --bin twyne-desktop && \\
  cargo test --locked --features ui-tests --manifest-path desktop/gpui/Cargo.toml <your test filter> && \\
  bun run desktop.gpui.parity --states <your,states>'
bun run desktop.gpui.job status <lane>          # running | finished N | none
bun run desktop.gpui.job logs <lane> --lines 80 # tail of the output
bun run desktop.gpui.job pull . --lane <lane>   # copy results + remote-job.log back, pause the lane
```

- A new lane starts from the warm snapshot (`twyne-gpui-warm`). It already has
  dependencies installed, the helper built and the `ui-tests` binary and
  tests compiled, so a run only rebuilds what you changed.
- Work in a loop. Commit a surface and start a job. Then port the next surface
  while the job runs. When the job finishes, pull it, fix whatever its tests
  or captures show, commit, and start the next job.
- Use one job per lane at a time. Run `bun run desktop.gpui.remote stop <lane>`
  when your lane is finished.
- Locally, run only cheap checks, such as
  `devenv shell -- cargo check --locked --no-default-features --manifest-path desktop/gpui/Cargo.toml`.
- If the runner itself fails, put the exact output in your report and keep
  coding. A runner failure is never a reason to stop.

## Keep going

Ending your turn early is the failure to avoid. One small commit and a final
report is not an acceptable outcome. Work through your checklist surface by
surface until every item is done, blocked (with the transport named) or not
applicable (with the reason). Only stop when that is true, or when you truly
cannot continue. In that case, commit first and list exactly what remains,
item by item.

'''
s=s[:start]+new+s[end:]
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

The port lanes all stopped early for the same reason: each made one small change, started its remote build in the foreground, waited on it, and ended its turn. That's fixed now. Ten lanes are back at work, and the other six never stopped.

**Fixes to the remote runner, on `feat/native-port-ai-audio`:**
- **Background builds** (`c3b6347f`). `bun run desktop.gpui.job start | status | logs | pull` starts a build or test on E2B and returns immediately, so a lane can keep coding while it runs. The lane rules now say never to run a remote command in the foreground, and they define "done" as every checklist item resolved.
- **Warm snapshot** (`c3b6347f`). One sandbox installs dependencies, builds the helper, and compiles the `ui-tests` binary and tests on the integration branch, then saves itself as `twyne-gpui-warm`. Every new lane boots from that copy and rebuilds only what it changed. The sync only rewrites files whose contents changed, so Cargo's build cache stays valid. The snapshot is building now.
- **Smaller sync** (`563cb939`). Each sync was uploading 893 MB, mostly `launch-videos/` and narration audio the build never reads. It's now about 110 MB. That upload was what had stalled the first warm attempt.

**What each restarted lane was told:**
- First merge the integration branch to pick up the new runner.
- Write its full progress file, with every item marked to-do.
- Then work surface by surface in a fixed order, starting a background build after each commit.

I also fixed specific mistakes:
- **insert** had marked all its items "blocked", which isn't what blocked means, and its Source fixture had drifted from the current web code.
- **account** had treated the unregistered production callback as a blocker. It now builds sign-in with a local loopback redirect and a fake identity provider for tests. Registering the production redirect URIs with Twyne and Not Organic is the one config step left for you. It also lands the `AccountSession` interface first, because desk, Live voice and settings are waiting on it.
- **settings** will start a build now, so its coordinator wiring gets compiled and tested.

**Committed so far in lane branches:**
- Saved AI settings now reach the coordinator.
- Selecting an active heading again toggles it back to body text.
- Escape closes the board.
- Split from Proof returns to Write.
- Source's Proof loading copy is used.
- The extra slash Link entry is gone.
- Drawer public pages open in the system browser.

None of these have been built or tested yet. That's what the background jobs are for.

Claude commonly uses {"effort":"max","fastMode":true}; Codex uses {"reasoningEffort":"max","serviceTier":"priority"}. Do not translate max to high or ignore unsupported settings: report a capability mismatch. Options inherit only for the same provider instance and model; explicit entries override individual values, and [] or {} clears them. Check the returned providerInstanceId, model, and options against the requested selection.


### Background work you wait on

Before you end your turn to wait for a background command or Monitor you started, such as tests, a build, or a CI wait, call `t3_background_wait` with its task ID. The thread then stays in the user's Working list until that task ends, instead of returning to them early. Do not mark a dev server, a watcher, or anything else you leave running.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: TaskStop
tools.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

tools.description: Needs an agent running inside a T3 thread. Choose providers and models from orchestrator_capabilities, which uses the same live catalog as the composer. Prefer native subagent tools for same-provider work only when they support the chosen model and no model options are requested or inherited. Use this for any model missing from the native tool, including same-provider work, for cross-provider work, or for explicitly T3-owned child tasks. For independent T3 delegated review rounds, call delegate_task again with the original brief, prior findings, responses, and unresolved objections in the task prompt. Track each round by its own taskId and use a distinct clientRequestId per round, stable across retries of that round. For a follow-up that needs the same child's conversation, use t3_thread_send on its childThreadId. Uncommitted edits are not copied; omitted isolation shares the parent checkout. Use delegate_task when model options are requested or the child keeps the parent's provider instance and model with nonempty inheritedOptions from orchestrator_capabilities, even for native-supported models. Native subagents cannot reliably apply T3 model options. Set target.options using advertised IDs: Claude {effort: 'max', fastMode: true}; Codex {reasoningEffort: 'max', serviceTier: 'priority'}. Check providerInstanceId, model, and options in the result. Provider/model and modes inherit unless overridden. Options inherit only for the same instance and model; explicit entries override individual values and [] or {} clears them. A requested runtimeMode must be one the target provider lists in orchestrator_capabilities runtimeModes; an inherited one steps down to the broadest mode it offers. Leave runtimeMode unset unless the user asks for a supervised child: approval-required and auto-accept-edits usually make the child wait for a person at each action that needs approval. Prefer mode='async' for long work; mode='wait' blocks until completion, a blocking question, a pending approval, or timeout. It grants no approval authority; decisions remain with the child's existing approval holder, and pending request tools answer questions only. The child keeps running and its completion still wakes this thread. timeoutMs on mode=wait is only the parent's wait budget and does not cancel the child. waitTimedOut on that wait call means the timeout fired; keep that taskId and read status on later task_status. An async child's completion wakes this thread through a notification, steered into active turns where supported or queued otherwise, so end the turn instead of polling or spawning watchers; use task_status only when the result is needed mid-turn.

The full desktop isn't at parity with the browser yet. All 16 port lanes are working again, and lanes are finally landing real commits. But nothing has been built or tested remotely yet, and no surface has a pixel score.

The lanes kept stopping after one small change for three reasons:
- **Commits hung.** `devenv shell -- git commit` never finished. The commit hook was pointing at a `prek` binary that no longer exists in the Nix store. I linked a current one into `~/.local/bin`, so plain `git commit` now passes the hook in about a second.
- **Remote jobs died.** The background-job command I'd written stayed tied to the request that started it, so it timed out. Jobs now use E2B's own background mode (`2ca0f85c`).
- **Key lookups collided.** Several lanes reading the E2B key from `skate` at once hit its database lock. The key is now read from a private cache file (`~/.config/twyne/e2b_api_key`, readable only by you), with `skate` as the fallback.

I told every lane to merge the fixes and commit with plain `git`. The four lanes that had stopped with uncommitted work were sent back to commit it first.

**Real progress in lane branches** (none built or tested yet):
- **Settings:** a checklist, removal that cancels when focus leaves, and saved AI settings connected to the coordinator.
- **Narration:** a player API with commands and queues, and playback tracked from the audio device.
- **Board-cast:** Escape closes the board, with a test.
- **Smaller fixes:** heading toggle-back, Split from Proof returning to Write, Proof loading copy, removal of the extra slash Link entry, and drawer public pages opening in the system browser.
- **Live voice:** a credential interface and handshake are staged. It found that LFM3-Audio doesn't have the realtime WebSocket API in `llama-server` yet. So the local Live option is built behind an interface and will show "not available on this device" until a runtime provides it.

**Building now:** the warm snapshot on E2B, the shared build that new lanes start from. Once it finishes, a lane's first remote build only recompiles what it changed.

**One thing you'll need to do:** the account lane is building sign-in with a local loopback redirect, so it doesn't need production setup to work. The production redirect URIs still have to be registered with Twyne and Not Organic. I'll give you the exact URIs when that lane lands.

content.thinking:
The user wants Railway instead of E2B for remote execution, likely due to cost or preference. I need to figure out what switching entails — whether to halt active E2B sandboxes immediately given they're currently in use by the lanes.

My plan is to build a Railway backend that matches the same job interface so lanes don't need command changes, then phase out E2B once Railway's confirmed working. Since lanes are designed to never block on a runner failure, stopping E2B now and routing job.ts to refuse E2B or redirect to Railway seems reasonable, though I need to think through whether Railway's PaaS model can even support the kind of arbitrary sandboxed execution E2B provides.

I'm weighing options: deploy a worker service on Railway exposing an HTTP API that accepts a tarball, runs a command, streams logs, and returns artifacts, backed by a cargo cache volume. Railway's Pro plan actually offers far more resources than E2B — up to 32 vCPU/32GB per service and 50GB volumes — and the CLI's `railway ssh` could let me exec commands directly into a running container, so I'm considering whether to run one large worker or multiple smaller services per lane given 16 lanes building concurrently.

Cost-wise, Railway charges roughly $0.028/vCPU-hr and $0.014/GB-hr, so an 8vCPU/16GB worker runs about $0.45/hr, comparable to E2B. For the design, I'm sketching a worker image with Nix/devenv plus a lightweight Bun HTTP job server exposing sync, job, status, logs, and pull endpoints, authenticated via a shared secret, with the Nix store itself needing to live on the persistent volume since it's large and costly to rebuild each time.

Since a volume can only mount one path, I'd mount it at /data, point CARGO_TARGET_DIR there, and bake the devenv toolchain into the image at build time by running the shell setup against the repo's devenv config. Cold builds per worker would take roughly 30 minutes at low concurrency but drop to around 10 minutes with more vCPUs, and I'm now weighing how many workers to run — likely one per lane, each with its own persistent volume.

Per-lane services avoid cache contention but I need to check Railway's limits on services per project and whether I should deploy via a shared image pushed to a registry versus building from the repo's Dockerfile directly. I'm also unsure what plan the user is on, so I should check their account details before committing to a 16-service architecture.

Given how central this runner infrastructure is, I'm weighing whether to build it myself or delegate to a Terra lane with a tight spec — Terra lanes have stalled before, but the remote runner lane previously delivered well, so delegation seems viable. Meanwhile I should figure out what to do about E2B: the user wants Railway instead, so I need to stop spinning up new E2B sandboxes without leaving lanes without any remote execution option in the interim.

I'll make `job start` return a message that the remote runner is moving to Railway, telling lanes to keep coding with local checks in the meantime. Running E2B sandboxes cost compute so I'll kill them now, but I'll keep the warm snapshot around cheaply until Railway is confirmed working, even though killing sandboxes mid-flight will disrupt lanes' in-progress jobs.

Now I need to look into Railway's capabilities — checking if there's SSH access via CLI, what the help output shows, and what the volume size limits and plan constraints look like.

  create      Create a sandbox and remember it as the active sandbox [aliases: new]

# Remote GPUI builds

Desktop builds, tests and captures run on Railway sandboxes in the
`twyne-gpui-builds` project. Each port lane has its own sandbox and runs
detached jobs, so an agent can start a build and keep working:

```sh
bun run desktop.gpui.job start . --lane <lane> --pull 'desktop/gpui/target/parity/**' -- <command...>
bun run desktop.gpui.job status <lane>          # running | finished N | interrupted | none
bun run desktop.gpui.job logs <lane> --lines 80 # tail of the output
bun run desktop.gpui.job pull . --lane <lane>   # copy --pull files and remote-job.log back
bun run desktop.gpui.job stop <lane>            # destroy the lane's sandbox
bun run desktop.gpui.job list                   # lanes and their sandboxes
```

## How it works

- **Running commands.** Commands run inside `devenv shell` in `/root/work`,
  so they use the pinned toolchain.
- **Syncing.** Each `start` streams the worktree's tracked and unignored files
  in. Launch videos and audio are left out. Files are compared by content, so
  unchanged files keep their timestamps and Cargo rebuilds only what the lane
  edited.
- **Checkpoints.** New lanes boot from the `twyne-gpui-warm` checkpoint. It
  already has dependencies installed, the document helper built, and the
  `ui-tests` binary and tests compiled.
  - Rebuild it after large changes on the integration branch with
    `bun desktop/gpui/tools/remote/railway.ts warm <worktree>`.
  - `twyne-gpui-base` holds just the toolchain: the apt libraries, Nix and
    devenv 2.4.0.
- **Lane records** live in `~/.config/twyne/railway-lanes.json`.
- **Idle timeout.** Sandboxes are destroyed after 120 idle minutes, so stop
  your lane when done.

The E2B runner (`run.ts`, `job.ts`, `warm.ts`, `rewarm.ts`) is retired and
refuses to start jobs.

content.text:
I've switched remote builds to Railway, and E2B is fully shut down. I stopped all 16 E2B sandboxes, and the old E2B runner now refuses to start jobs, so none can start again by accident.

The new runner is `desktop/gpui/tools/remote/railway.ts` (commit `e1fe8fcf` on `feat/native-port-ai-audio`). Lanes keep using the same commands (`bun run desktop.gpui.job start | status | logs | pull | stop | list`), so their briefs didn't need rewriting.

- **Project:** a new, separate Railway project, `twyne-gpui-builds`, so these sandboxes stay apart from your live services. Each sandbox has 8 vCPU, 7 GB RAM and 29 GB disk.
- **Checkpoints:** `twyne-gpui-base` is saved and holds the toolchain: system libraries, Nix and devenv 2.4.0. `twyne-gpui-warm` adds dependencies, the document helper, and the built `ui-tests` binary and tests. It's building now, and every lane will boot from it once it's ready.
- **Jobs:** each lane gets its own sandbox. A job starts in the background and returns immediately, and syncing only rewrites changed files. A sandbox is destroyed after 120 idle minutes.
- **Checked so far:** upload, download and detached runs all work on a real sandbox. A test job got as far as entering the project's devenv shell.

Two Railway quirks the runner works around:
- Commands run without `$USER` set, so Nix doesn't load until the runner sets `USER=root`.
- The `--project` and `--environment` flags have to come before `--`, otherwise they become part of the command.

Railway labels sandboxes as experimental, and its template builder fails without saying which step failed. So I set up the toolchain inside a live sandbox and saved it as a checkpoint instead.

All 16 lanes have been told to merge the switch. Most picked it up mid-turn, and the idle ones will get it at the start of their next turn. Until the warm checkpoint exists, a lane's first job builds from scratch, so they're starting jobs and carrying on coding. I've also updated memory: Railway is the preferred remote runner, along with these setup details.

The "cancelled" messages from those two lanes were older turns, replaced when I sent the Railway switch. Both lanes are still running.

I'll report when the warm checkpoint is ready, and as lanes land commits and pixel scores.

The desktop isn't at parity with the browser yet, and no surface has a pixel score so far. The 16 port lanes are now committing steadily, but none of that work has been built or tested yet, so every checklist still shows 0 items done.

**Biggest commit runs this round:**
- **Desk** (about 20 commits): My Desk now opens a native desk with local writing activity, pace and recent work. Writer patterns and a forecast line are partly done, and you can delete the local activity record after confirming.
- **Typst views** (about 20 commits): Source draft and save-error alerts, proof zoom and PDF controls, Split keeping its mode when you switch workspaces, and Zen and Split capture states.
- **Instruments** (about 19 commits): the Sentence Bench, with wording checks and comparison, candidate sources, and context.
- **Dossier** (14 commits): starter documents now match the web's title-only version. Format suggestions now list every match and have the chevron.
- **Editor input** (10 commits): double-click and triple-click selection with drag, more shortcuts, and tests for undo grouping and typing non-ASCII characters.
- **Live voice** (8 commits): a hosted connection over a websocket (new crate: `tungstenite`) with a fake-gateway test, a signed-out desk the Talk button opens, and audio, transcript and delegation pieces that aren't connected to each other yet.

**Conflict fix** (`dbe11e30`). Before merging anything, I test-merged all 16 lane branches. Nine collided on the same three hard-coded lists of capture-state names. Each lane now keeps its own list in `tools/parity/states.d/<lane>.json`, and the native check and harness read the base list plus all of those. A few conflicts remain in `app.rs`, `room_layout.rs` and `Cargo.lock`, between live-voice, account and desk. I've asked those lanes to keep their host edits in one marked block each, so I can resolve them mechanically when I merge.

**"Blocked" items that weren't real blockers.** Lanes kept marking work as blocked when it was really their own job: settings marked language as blocked on native locale support, and dossier marked the conversation's host connection. I've told every lane that "blocked" means only something outside this repo, like a production registration. Anything native they build themselves.

**Builds on Railway.** About 11 lane sandboxes are compiling from scratch, and the warm checkpoint build restarted at 02:50 UTC. Once it's saved, new lane sandboxes start from it, so they only rebuild what changed. I'll merge each lane into the integration branch once its remote tests pass, so lanes can use each other's work: Cast speech calling the narration player, and desk, Live voice and hosted AI using the account session.
